question: A \(16\)-quart radiator is filled with water. Four quarts are removed and replaced with pure antifreeze liquid. Then four quarts of the mixture are removed and replaced with pure antifreeze. This is done a third and a fourth time. The fractional part of the final mixture that is water is:
solution:
Track the water, since each refill adds only antifreeze. Using the usual assumption that the liquid is uniformly mixed before each withdrawal, removing \(4\) of the \(16\) quarts removes \(1/4\) of the water then present. Thus each complete withdrawal and refill leaves \(3/4\) of the previous water amount.

The radiator returns to \(16\) quarts after every refill, so its water fraction is also multiplied by \(3/4\) each time. Starting with water fraction \(1\), after four replacements the fraction is
\[
1\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac34
=\frac{81}{256}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\frac{81}{256}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

edges.scope: fraction as a count of unit fractional parts

edges.reason: The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.

The endpoint provides explicit quantity-modeling experience that can help translate a fraction-of-a-whole story into an expression. Price and speed formulas do not define a fractional part, so the benefit is preparation only. This final scoped judgment does not treat a prior native acceptance of Claude's rejection as an accepted dependency.
edges.scope: Prior experience representing total, part and multiplicative relationships in application problems
